extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and resolving rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102/103 and double patenting where prior art may be disqualified due to common ownership or joint research agreements (including evidence and effective-date rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 and double patenting rejections by common ownership and terminal disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 may be overcome and double patenting rejection may be overcome if inventions X and XY are commonly owned and all requirements of 37 CFR 1.130 and 1.321 are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimer filed under 37 CFR 1.321(c) can obviate double patenting rejection if common ownership exists; examples show provisional rejections when subject matter and prior art are pending applications. Examiner practice: provisional 102(e)/103 rejection may be made when prior art is a pending application; such rejections can be withdrawn if evidence of common ownership and any required terminal disclaimer are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional nature of 102(e)/103 rejections when prior art is a pending application
rubrics_metrics.description: In situations where the prior art and the subject matter are pending applications, the examiner may make a provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 (and provisional double patenting rejections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rejections are 'provisional' because the subject matter and the alleged prior art are pending applications; the provisional rejection may be withdrawn if the applicant establishes common ownership or meets terminal disclaimer requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory 35 U.S.C. 103(c) prior-art disqualification rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter developed by another person, which qualifies as prior art only under one or more of subsections (e), (f), and (g) of section 102, shall not preclude patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the claimed invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory foundation for excluding certain prior art from obviousness rejections; it applies only to obviousness under 103, not to anticipation under 102 or to double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint research agreement conditions for 103(c) disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of 103(c), subject matter developed by another person and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person if: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application for patent for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. All three conditions must be satisfied for the 103(c) exclusion based on a joint research agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: 103(c) applies only to obviousness and only to 102(e),(f),(g) prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) applies only to consideration of prior art for purposes of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103. It does not apply to or affect subject matter which is applied in a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 or a double patenting rejection. If the subject matter qualifies as prior art under any other subsection of 35 U.S.C. 102 (e.g., 102(a) or (b)) it will not be disqualified under 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on 103(c) to overcome anticipation under 102 or double patenting rejections; use 37 CFR 1.78(c) and MPEP § 804 guidance for double patenting and terminal disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for disqualifying prior art under 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent applicant or patentee urging that subject matter is disqualified has the burden of establishing that the prior art is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent proper evidence of disqualification, the appropriate rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) using prior art under 102(e),(f), or (g) should be made. The fact that a reference and the application have the same assignee is not by itself sufficient; there must be evidence (e.g., statement) that common ownership existed 'at the time the invention was made.' The burden resides on the person urging disqualification, not the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective-date and scope rules (AIPA and CREATE Act) for 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1999 AIPA changes to 103(c) (effective for applications filed on or after Nov 29, 1999) and the CREATE Act (effective for patents granted on or after Dec 10, 2004) altered which applications/patents are governed by the amended 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CREATE Act redesignated and expanded 103(c) and made it effective for patents granted on or after Dec 10, 2004 (including many earlier-filed applications that were pending on that date). For reexamination proceedigns, determine whether the patent was granted on or after Dec 10, 2004 to see if the CREATE amendment applies. The amendments do not affect patents granted before Dec 10, 2004.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'commonly owned' for 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'commonly owned' means wholly owned by the same person(s) or organization(s) at the time the invention was made; common ownership requires 100% ownership of both the subject matter/reference and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ownership is less than 100% for either the reference or the claimed invention, common ownership does not exist. Examples illustrate parent/subsidiary, joint venture, partial ownership, and licenses. A license where basic ownership rights are retained does not defeat ownership. The requirement prevents obtaining ownership after the invention to disqualify prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence sufficient to establish common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement by the applicant(s) or an attorney/agent of record that the application and the reference were, at the time the invention was made, owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person is sufficient evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 'Guidelines Setting Forth a Modified Policy Concerning the Evidence of Common Ownership' (1241 O.G. 96, Dec. 26, 2000). Applicant/representative statements are sufficient because of their duty of candor and good faith. The common ownership must be shown to exist at the time the later invention was made; a present statement of common ownership alone is not sufficient (In re Onda).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure regarding 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior filed copending national or international application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application, and the prior filed application must disclose the named inventor's invention claimed in at least one claim of the later filed application as provided by 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So long as the applications have at least one inventor in common and other requirements are met, the Office will permit a claim for 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit without additional submissions regarding inventorship differences. The examiner must examine the earlier filed application to determine common inventorship and other 120 requirements and may permit the 120 claim without examining the earlier application's disclosure/support unless necessary (e.g., intervening reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstated practice of double patenting rejections among commonly owned applications
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the Director has reinstated in appropriate circumstances the practice of rejecting claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities on the grounds of double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such double patenting rejections can be overcome in appropriate circumstances by filing terminal disclaimers; this practice is judicially authorized (e.g., In re Bowers). Use MPEP § 804 and 37 CFR 1.78(c) for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recapture doctrine caution in reissue applications
rubrics_metrics.description: For reissue applications, the doctrine of recapture may prevent the presentation of claims in the reissue application that were amended or cancelled from the application which matured into the patent for which reissue is being sought, if the claims were amended or cancelled to distinguish the claimed invention from 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 prior art which was not able to be excluded under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) in the application that issued as a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner determines recapture may apply in the reissue application, consultation with the Office of Patent Legal Administration should be initiated via the Technology Center Special Program Examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of 'made' for purposes of common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is 'made' when conception is complete (e.g., as defined in Mergenthaler v. Scudder and In re Tansel; Pfaff v. Wells Elecs. clarifies 'ready for patenting' standard). Common ownership must exist at the time the invention was made to obviate 102/103 rejections via 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must look to facts of each case to determine ownership at the time of invention. Common ownership at the time of invention may be established irrespective of whether invention was made in the U.S. or abroad; however, other statutes (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 104) may govern foreign activity issues in interference proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability limits for older applications/patents (pre-1999 and pre-2004)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications filed prior to November 29, 1999 and granted as patents prior to December 10, 2004, the subject matter disqualified under 103(c) was strictly limited to subject matter qualifying only under 102(f) or 102(g) and commonly owned at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information learned from or transmitted to persons outside the organization was not disqualified as prior art under those earlier provisions. For reexamination of patents granted prior to Dec 10, 2004, determine which version of 103(c) (1999 or 2004 changes) applies based on filing/grant dates as explained in the MPEP.
